objects: SNP genotype; measured phenotypes; phenotype linear combinations
assumptions: single-phenotype GWAS or a phenotype fixed a priori as a function of traits
conclusion: Testing flexible phenotype linear combinations may reveal genetic associations hidden by single-phenotype or fixed-function analyses.
scope: Authors stated motivation; potential discovery rather than a universal power guarantee.
span: Modelling the association between linear combinations of phenotypes and the genotypes at each SNP may uncover genetic association hidden to both single phenotype GWAS and those based on a priori defining a phenotype as a fixed function of traits. Such an approach circumvents the problems of phenotype definition by enabling association of genotype with flexible linear combinations of robust measurements, and could potentially be exploited by biologists and clinicians to define phenotypes that better reflect underlying biological processes.

objects: ordinal SNP allele count X; K phenotype predictors Y
assumptions: genotype is an ordered allele count
conclusion: MultiPhen reverses regression and models SNP genotype as the outcome of proportional odds logistic regression on multiple phenotypes.
scope: One SNP at a time; conditional ordinal regression model.
span: In our MultiPhen approach we invert the regression so that the SNP genotypes, X, become the dependent variable, and the K phenotypes under study become the predictor variables. The genotype data is an allele count and is therefore modelled using ordinal regression; we use proportional odds logistic regression.
location: multiphen | journal OA version | Materials and Methods > MultiPhen Approach

objects: individual phenotype vector Yi; genotype vector Xi; Xig in {0,1,2}
assumptions: phenotypes and genotypes correspond to the same individual
conclusion: The defined input consists of individual-level measurements of K phenotypes and genotype allele counts across G SNPs.
scope: Input definition in the main method; no summary-statistics implementation is stated.
span: We let Yi = {Yi1, …, YiK} denote the phenotype data corresponding to K phenotypes for an individual i and Xi = {Xi1, …, XiG} denote their genotype data at G SNPs, where Xig ε {0,1,2}.
location: multiphen | journal OA version | Materials and Methods > MultiPhen Approach

conclusion: MultiPhen identifies the phenotype linear combination most associated with genotype at each SNP.
scope: Association and phenotype-combination discovery; no causal identification guarantee.
span: We introduce a new method, MultiPhen, that rapidly performs GWAS on multiple phenotypes by identifying the linear combination of the phenotypes most associated with genotype at each SNP.

objects: joint null beta_g1 = ... = beta_gK = 0; likelihood ratio statistic
assumptions: one SNP and K phenotype coefficients
conclusion: MultiPhen tests the joint zero-coefficient null with a likelihood ratio test at each SNP.
scope: Association-testing procedure; the numerical coefficient-fitting algorithm is unspecified in this passage.
span: At each SNP g = 1,…,G we use a likelihood ratio test to test the null hypothesis βg1 = … = βgK =0.
location: multiphen | journal OA version | Materials and Methods > MultiPhen Approach

assumptions: phenotypes enter as predictors in the reversed ordinal regression
conclusion: The authors state that the model imposes no phenotype-distribution assumption and accommodates binary and continuous measurements.
scope: Stated model property; not an unconditional finite-sample calibration theorem.
span: This model makes no assumption on the phenotype distribution and so can accommodate both binary and continuous measurements.

objects: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium; likelihood ratio association test
conclusion: The association test does not assume Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
scope: No assertion here about robustness to every form of genotype-model misspecification.
span: This test does not assume Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium.
location: multiphen | journal OA version | Materials and Methods > MultiPhen Approach

conclusion: The authors describe MultiPhen as making no prior assumptions about the nature of genetic effects on the phenotypes.
scope: Qualitative statement about effect patterns; no Bayesian effect-prior distribution or penalty is specified.
span: MultiPhen should be considered a discovery tool for application to multiple correlated phenotypes that makes no prior assumptions about the nature of the genetic effects on the phenotypes.

objects: SNP genotype outcome; phenotype linear combination; CCA
assumptions: CCA as implemented by Ferreira and Purcell; one SNP at a time
conclusion: MultiPhen and CCA test the most genotype-associated phenotype linear combination, while MultiPhen models genotype as ordinal and CCA treats it as normal.
scope: Comparison of genotype models and association targets.
span: MultiPhen and CCA (as implemented by Ferreira and Purcell [15]) both test the linear combination of the phenotypes most associated with the genotypes of a SNP against a null hypothesis of no association, but while CCA treats the genotypes as normally distributed MultiPhen appropriately models the genotypes as ordinal.

objects: CCA statistic; reversed linear-regression F-test; MANOVA
assumptions: CCA applied one SNP at a time as in Ferreira and Purcell
conclusion: The paper identifies single-SNP CCA with reversed linear-regression F-testing and MANOVA, extending its observed type-I error inflation to these comparators.
scope: Comparator equivalence stated by the authors; MultiPhen itself is not asserted equivalent to MANOVA.
span: We note that when CCA is applied one-SNP-at-a-time, as in Ferreira and Purcell [15], its test statistic is equivalent to an F-test in a linear regression model with SNP genotypes as outcome and to a MANOVA test, and therefore these approaches have the same inflation of the type 1 error rate in the scenarios considered here.
location: multiphen | journal OA version | Results > Type 1 Error Rate Assessed by Simulation

objects: null association tests; common and rare variants; continuous and binary phenotypes
assumptions: the simulated scenarios examined in the paper
conclusion: In the examined simulations MultiPhen had appropriate type-I error across the tested variant frequencies and phenotype distributions.
scope: Empirical calibration in tested scenarios; no universal theoretical calibration guarantee.
span: We demonstrated that the MultiPhen model provides appropriate type 1 error rate when applied to both common and rare variants, non-normal continuous phenotypes and binary phenotypes.

objects: genetic-effect direction; phenotype correlation; univariate comparator
conclusion: The single-phenotype approach can be slightly more powerful when genetic effects agree with phenotype correlation.
scope: Simulation-based relative-power limitation; examples include equal effects on highly correlated phenotypes and one affected uncorrelated phenotype.
span: If the genetic effects are consistent with the correlation between the two phenotypes, then the single phenotype approach is slightly more powerful, for example, if the variant has the same effect on two highly correlated phenotypes, or only affects one of two uncorrelated phenotypes.
location: multiphen | journal OA version | Results > Statistical Power Assessed by Simulation

objects: P1; P2; G; beta2/beta1; phenotype correlation r
assumptions: two phenotypes both with variance 1; P2 conditionally independent of G given P1
conclusion: The authors characterize the worst-power setting as conditional independence of the second phenotype and genotype given the first, corresponding to beta2/beta1 = r for standardized phenotypes.
scope: Two-phenotype theoretical characterization; no general power bound or formal theorem is supplied.
span: We note that, from a theoretical perspective, the power of MultiPhen using two phenotypes P1 and P2, is worst when the association of P2 with genotype G is entirely explained by P1, that is when P2 is conditionally independent of G given P1. We show that this corresponds to the situation in which the ratio of the effect sizes β2/β1 = r (the correlation between the phenotypes), assuming P1 and P2 both have a variance of 1 (see Methods).
